key_points: Vilas Patankar's tribute "V. B. Karnik—A Tribute" recounts Karnik surviving a knife attack decades earlier when colleague Wamanrao Kulkarni intervened, his direction of Acharya Kripalani's 1962 campaign against Krishna Menon, and his decades as Honorary Secretary of the Democratic Research Service and editor of Freedom First; a sidebar by Minoo Masani praises the dignified manner of his death at 82.

Bhanu Pratap Singh's "Indian Agriculture—A Stunted Giant" blames the Nehru-Mahalanobis strategy of capital-intensive industrialisation for stunting Indian agriculture, citing Punjab's outsized productivity as proof of unrealised potential and calling farmers "captive producers and captive consumers."

In an essay headed "Traditions and Trends in Marathi Newspapers," Minoo Masani recalls Nehru once telling him he "thinks like a modern man" and argues India's readiness for the 21st century is a matter of human attitudes and institutions, citing postal delays, bank inefficiency, superstition, and the absence of a common civil code and link language.
The issue opens by dedicating itself to the memory of V. B. Karnik, the Democratic Research Service's Honorary Secretary, who died on 5 November 1985.

The issue also marks Minoo Masani's eightieth birthday, noting a felicitation dinner and the presentation of a festschrift volume, "Freedom and Dissent," with congratulatory notes from J. R. D. Tata and Senator Giovanni Malagodi of the Liberal International.
The regular "With Many Voices" and "Of Cabbages & Kings" columns address contemporary Indian politics, media freedom, and human-rights concerns including the 1984 anti-Sikh violence and "black laws."

S.P. Aiyar's "Recapturing the Lost Spirit of the University" contrasts the post-Independence university ideal with 1986 decay, citing growth from 27 to 140 universities between 1950-51 and 1982-83, and proposes that students pay the full cost of their education to restore accountability.

Padmini Murty's "Women's Education — A Perspective" documents that only 30 of 100 girls enrolled in class I reach class V, a gendered concentration of women students in arts and medicine over engineering, and calls for literacy programmes tailored to women's socio-economic circumstances.

Minoo Masani's "Dangerous 'Carelessness'" column satirises the Maharashtra government's habit of declaring ad hoc holidays, notes the irony of the pre-1980 rule barring diplomats from marrying foreigners given Rajiv Gandhi's own foreign-born wife, and mocks his warning against the "alien concept of pragmatism."

Giovanni Malagodi, President of Liberal International, in "The Maintenance of Freedom" argues free states now use low-visibility administrative controls on information in place of overt censorship, and frames the UNESCO "New World Information Order" debate as Third World governments' complaints often masking their own domestic media monopolies.

The issue marks Freedom First's entry into its 35th year of publication with a redesigned layout, and its "Of Cabbages and Kings" column carries obituary notes on Masti Venkatesa Iyengar and Sophia Wadia alongside commentary on the Arwal massacre and the Tagore centenary.
A second symposium strand, "Raids on Personal Freedom," carries contributions from founder Minoo Masani and M.R. Pai on civil-liberties concerns of the day.

Manohar Malgonkar's "J.R.D. Tata – A Profile in Trusteeship" reviews Tata's compiled speeches in Keynote, crediting him with founding Tata Air Mail (forerunner of Air India), holding India's first pilot's certificate, and choosing in 1938 to dedicate himself to running the Tata empire over deeper involvement in the freedom struggle.

In "The Masani Viewpoint," Minoo Masani criticises the Supreme Court review sought against the ruling that anthem-singing is not compulsory, broadly endorses Vasant Sathe's public criticism of the public sector as an unaccountable "holy cow," and recalls his personal acquaintance with both Subhas Chandra Bose and Mahatma Gandhi.

The symposium "The State and the Arts," reprinting papers from an August 1986 Leslie Sawhny Programme seminar in Goa, lays out the classical-liberal premise that the State's role in cultural life should be minimal, confined to education and preservation rather than direct patronage.

S.V. Raju's "The Arts on a Leash" reports disappointment at the seminar's lack of consensus on state arts funding and broadcasting autonomy, criticising the government's plan to raise Zonal Arts Council funding from 12 crores to Rs. 51 crores as a scheme for artificial "national integration."

Nissim Ezekiel argues government cannot legitimately claim to speak for Society and Culture, and, citing Hugh Jenkins on Britain's Arts Council, contends state art awards raise controversy without raising standards.

Govind Talwalkar traces the tension between the state and literature through Plato and Hans Morgenthau, blaming India's textbook nationalisation and the underperforming National Book Trust translation scheme for undermining serious private literary publishing.

Krishen Khanna surveys state involvement in the visual arts from royal patronage through colonial "Victorian" academic art to the Lalit Kala Akademi, recounting censorship episodes involving F.N. Souza and Akbar Padamsee.

Mehra Masani argues against state monopoly of All India Radio and Doordarshan, rebutting Rajiv Gandhi's claim that India is "not ready for autonomy" and citing the restrictive 1967 AIR Code and the absence of any constitutional safeguard against political interference in broadcasting.

M.V. Kamath's "The Face of Indian Communalism" argues most riots are economically rather than religiously driven, using the 1982-83 Baroda riots as his central case study, and concludes that reconciling India-Pakistan relations is "the key" to ending communalism.

Kamila Tyabji's "The Roots of National (Dis)Integration" recounts a 1968 episode organising a mixed stitching class in Taloja village where Muslim women refused to cross into a "Hindu mohalla," and proposes multi-lingual, mixed-community schools as a structural remedy.

Dilip Simeon's "Communalism: A Symptom of Fascism" argues Indian communalism is better understood as "Brahmanical fascism," a domestic variant of fascist populism tracing to Bankim Chattopadhyay and Tilak, and holds that Partition was substantially its product.

K.F. Rustomji's "Who Are the Fanatics?" draws on fifty years of policing to argue rioters are rarely genuine believers but cynical operators — lawyers, businessmen, and politicians — who invoke religion for personal or political gain.

Aloo J. Dastur's "Are the Minorities Too Much With Us?" catalogues the proliferation of Indian commissions on minorities and backward classes, arguing they have "whetted minority appetites, not satisfying them," while surveying rising Hindu majority anxiety evidenced by the VHP and the Ekatmata Yatra.
The issue's regular "With Many Voices" and "Of Cabbages and Kings" columns carry press clippings and short editorial notes on black money, leadership, and defaulting politicians.

The editors' note explains the issue's focus on "The Right to Live and the Right to Die with Dignity," drawn from the Sixth Biennial Conference of the World Federation of Right to Die Societies held in Bombay in November 1986, and cites Bhishma's chosen death in the Mahabharata as an Indian precedent.

Geeta Doctor's "Acoustic Trauma" satirises a genteel anti-noise-pollution march by the Environmental Society of Madras, ending on the irony of blaring devotional loudspeakers resuming the moment the march concludes.

Sir Edmund Hillary's "Life or Death — Not an Easy Decision" draws on his mother's death, a near-fatal 1953 Everest crevasse fall, and Sherpa children born disabled to argue no one should be kept alive as "a helpless cabbage" once terminally ill or in great pain.

Minoo Masani's "The Right to Choose" surveys the Netherlands' judge-led euthanasia framework and Indian legal progress via Justice Sachar's and the Bombay High Court's rulings, and cites Prof. Sadanand Varde's bill granting doctors immunity for honouring a patient's wish for passive euthanasia.

Alexander Capron's address sets out three "perils" facing the right-to-die movement: the gap between legal rights and clinical practice, the risk of a "right to die" becoming a perceived "duty to die," and passive euthanasia sliding into active, physician-assisted killing.
The issue frames its choice of theme as offering readers "some relief" against a backdrop of budget disappointment, the President-Prime Minister controversy, and violence in Punjab.

Sharad Joshi's "The Need for a Second Republic" argues the 1950 Republic is dying as power has concentrated in the Prime Minister at the expense of the states, judiciary and Parliament, tracing Punjab's crisis to economic exploitation of Sikh farmers and calling for radical decentralisation and a two-term cap on the premiership.

Minoo Masani's "The President's Powers" defends the President's genuine constitutional checks on the Prime Minister, quoting Articles 74, 75 and 111, and criticises the Emergency-era 42nd Amendment for supporting an anti-pluralist reading of majority rule.

D. V. Gundappa's "Liberalism in India," reprinted for his birth centenary, argues Indian liberalism grew as a re-articulation of the Hindu concept of Dharma rather than a European import, tracing its modern genealogy from Rammohan Roy through Mahadev Govind Ranade.

The regular "Of Cabbages and Kings" column comments on political scandals, the Radical Humanist journal's fiftieth anniversary, the Uniform Civil Code debate, and the death of former Prime Minister Charan Singh.
The issue reprints a statement by the Dalai Lama on Tibet and honours the late administrator A. D. Gorwala.

R.M. Lala's "Leadership for the 21st Century" argues India's post-independence leadership has not matched the Constituent Assembly generation, invoking Akbar's shift from conquest to consent and calling for devolution of power from the Prime Minister's Office to the Cabinet and states.

Ratna Naidu's "The Conditions which Generate Communal Conflict" identifies three structural conditions generating communal conflict — threatened class privilege, adverse demographic spread, and accumulated historical hatred — using Jat Sikh landlord anxieties after the Green Revolution as her Punjab case study.

Lionel Fernandes's "De-mythifying Minority Rights" argues minority protection cannot extend to fundamentalist practices exempt from rational civil regulation, and proposes a voluntary, secular National Civil Code as a pilot step.

A.H. Doctor's "An Industrial Policy for the 21st Century" names four pillars of industrial policy — technology transfer, import substitution, quality improvement via competition, and manpower planning — and flags computer software as a strategic industry that could reverse brain drain.

Kamal Wadhwa's "The 'Dog' that Barks" surveys public reaction to Ram Jethmalani's month-long public interrogation of Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi over the Bofors affair, including former CM A.R. Antulay's "barking dog" defence and the ensuing "canine jurisprudence" debate.

Minoo Masani's regular column publishes writer Rama Swarup's account of persecution under the Official Secrets Act, reflects on the poorly-attended 45th anniversary of Quit India, and discusses Swiss bank secrecy, arguing (via A.G. Noorani) that India's own laxity, not Berne, blocks disclosure of illicit deposits.

Jayaprakash Narayan's "Sardar Patel – A Re-appraisal" recounts his own past opposition to Patel as a defender of capitalism, credits Patel's integration of the princely states (which even Khrushchev admired) and his prophetic 1950 letter warning Nehru of Chinese designs on Tibet, and faults Nehru for tolerating corruption once Patel's discipline was gone.

Arvind Deshpande's "A National Caretaker Government" argues repeated electoral mandates have produced a corrosive "choicelessness," and proposes a temporary, President-installed National Caretaker Government of talents to bridge the crisis, distinct from both an Emergency and a "palace revolution."

B.K. Nehru's "The 'Indianisation' of the Constitution" argues decades of practice have eroded the Presidency's informational role, the bureaucracy's Westminster-style independence, and the individual MP's ability to check the executive, calling for constitutional revision to build more durable checks.

Minoo Masani's "The Essence of Democracy – Not Majority Rule" argues unlimited majority rule can itself be tyrannical, laying out five conditions for genuine democracy and favourably citing Switzerland's proportional, cantonal model over India's "first past the post" system.

The issue opens with a reappraisal of Sardar Patel paired with an extract from his November 1950 letter warning Nehru of Chinese expansionism, and closes its rendered pages with a tribute to Nobel laureate Joseph Brodsky by Nissim Ezekiel.

A.N. Dalal's "Violence, Civilization and Democratic Values" argues mass violence is chiefly learned through social conditioning and media desensitisation, treating dowry deaths and child labour as forms of "passive" social violence, and invokes Gandhi, Martin Luther King and Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan as models of non-violent response.

A companion book-note by Dalal reviews Elias Canetti's Crowds and Power, summarising Canetti's theory of the destructive "survivor" who feels empowered by mass death and calling the book's neglect in India "one of the surprising scandals of our decade."

Louella Lobo Prabhu traces the roots of violence in Indian politics from mythic and historical precedent through the abrogation of princely privy purses and the "reverse discrimination" effects of caste reservations, concluding India has strayed from the standards of Ashoka and Gandhi under its own elected governments.

The issue's coverage of the 'Riddles' controversy reproduces a primary-source extract from B.R. Ambedkar's Riddles in Hinduism, presenting his critique of Rama's treatment of Sita after her rescue as incompatible with "ordinary human kindness."

A reprinted extract of Ambedkar's 25 November 1949 Constituent Assembly speech, "Safeguarding Our Democracy," warns that India could lose its hard-won independence again through internal treachery and urges constitutional methods over the "Grammar of Anarchy."

A Bombay seminar statement, "Tibet Struggles for Freedom," condemns China's occupation of Tibet, records over 87,000 Tibetans killed suppressing the national uprising, and endorses the Dalai Lama's Five Point Peace Plan.

The "Of Cabbages & Kings" round-up covers Milovan Djilas's rare 1987 interview on continuing crisis in communist systems, opposition-called Bharat Bandhs, Singapore's press restrictions, and South Korea's state-directed "Chaebol" economy.

Milovan Djilas's "Is Soviet Ideology Really Changing" argues Gorbachev's reforms are changes made by the ruling oligarchy, too limited to be systemic change, though he credits glasnost as a real if modest achievement exposing "the destructive force of Brezhnev's bureaucratism."

Bernard Levin's "On Guard — or Gorbachev will Tickle You Red" skewers Western credulity toward glasnost, arguing Gorbachev differs from his predecessors chiefly in intelligence rather than any liberal inclination, and lists continuing Soviet abuses including the Gulag and censorship.

Geeta Doctor's satirical "Glass Nose Anyone?" imagines a bewildered global "agent" failing to get a coherent answer about what glasnost and perestroika actually mean, ending with a grieving Muscovite's pun rejecting "Glasnost."

Ramnath Narayanswamy's survey frames 1988 as an "acid test" year for Gorbachev and works country by country through Eastern Europe, from Hungary's debt crisis and Poland's stalled reform to Ceausescu's unreformed Romania and Yugoslav economists proposing a full market economy.

Vasundhara Mohan's report on the 19th CPSU Conference, the first in 47 years, credits glasnost with exposing official misdeeds like the Yuri Churbanov corruption case, and profiles Boris Yeltsin as the reform camp's most impatient, demoted figure.
The issue also carries editorial commentary on India's own political scene, including the withdrawal of the 1988 Defamation Bill and the fragility of the newly formed National Front.

C. Rajagopalachari's 1964 reprint "The Value of Traditional Values" argues traditional values such as honesty and compassion are evolutionary products essential to human survival that secular law cannot substitute for.

The Dalai Lama's "Religious Values and Human Society" presents compassion, not doctrine, as religion's essential core, arguing good motivation rather than religious affiliation determines whether politics and other fields serve or harm humanity.

A. B. Shah's posthumously reprinted "Religion and Society" contrasts Gandhi's and Maulana Azad's differing approaches to reforming Hinduism and Islam, arguing Gandhi succeeded partly because prior Hindu reformers since Rammohan Roy had already done the "spadework."

Abe Solomon's "Religion and Politics" rejects Minoo Masani's call for more "Dharma in politics," arguing India's sarva-dharma-samabhava conception of secularism corrupts true secularism by tacitly endorsing discriminatory religious practices.

M. R. Sundareswaran's "Ban and be Damned!" chronicles the October 1988 banning of Salman Rushdie's The Satanic Verses under pressure from MP Syed Shahabuddin, casting it as electorally motivated appeasement and a betrayal of constitutional free-speech guarantees.

Sidebar reprints accompanying the Rushdie coverage include Soli Sorabjee's op-ed against the ban, an account of Premchand's own colonial-era censorship, Minoo Masani's recollection of Indira Gandhi's Emergency-era ban on his son Zareer's biography of her, and Nehru's essay "On the Banning of Books."

Jiban K. Mukhopadhyay's lead essay argues non-plan expenditure has permanently outstripped revenue, describing a "statistical juggler" masking the true deficit and projecting government debt reaching Rs. 2.6 lakh crores by March 1990.

D. R. Pendse's "The Internal Debt Trap — Too Close for Comfort" warns India will enter a self-perpetuating debt trap by 1992, when annual interest exceeds new borrowing, and urges selling up to 49% of shares in profitable public enterprises.

P. R. Brahmananda applies a "canon of minimal fiscal viability" to find the Central Government fails even to cover its inescapable expenditures, judging it, by the RBI's own criteria, "very chronically sick."

N. A. Palkhivala's Budget speech calls the 1989-90 Union Budget "purely an exercise in political symbolism" that reverses the government's own 1985 liberalisation planks, and calls for statutory borrowing limits under Article 292.

Y. Sivaji's "An Economy in Dire Straits" lays out a twelve-point corrective programme — expenditure control, a hiring moratorium, public-sector "perestroika," and a higher income-tax exemption limit — against a widening trade deficit and depreciating rupee.

C. Rajagopalachari's reprinted 1960 essay "Deficit Financing" traces chronic Indian inflation to deficit financing since 1955-56, arguing only restoring balance between production and money flow can cure rising prices.

Swaminathan S. Anklesaria Aiyar's "A Tale of Two Deficits" argues liberalisation has newly linked India's budget and trade deficits, attributing the import surge to deficit-financing-driven over-consumption rather than loosened sectoral controls.

Dharma Vira's "The Civil Service — Then & Now" credits Sardar Patel as architect of the all-India services and Article 311 safeguards, and argues the civil service's original integrity and esprit de corps have eroded as officers pursued personal advancement.

L.K. Jha's satirical "Mr. Red Tape" personifies bureaucratic obstruction as a character who explains his caution as rational self-preservation, since "sins of commission are easier to detect than sins of omission."

J.B. D'Souza's "Bumbling Officialdom" uses Bombay's 1981–2001 Draft Development Plan, delayed for years amid proliferating advisory committees, to ask whether civil servants are merely government servants or public servants with obligations to society at large.

H.M. Patel's "What is Wrong with our Bureaucracy?" argues today's civil servants behave as masters rather than servants, calling for "a total revolution" in their self-conception of duty while locating the real solution in voters' willingness to remove bad government.

A.G. Sivaramakrishnan's reminiscence recounts British ICS officer Philip Mason publicly rebuking a Brigadier for disrespecting a junior Indian assistant, framing such officers as embodiments of an administrative ethos India has since lost.

The editorial and regular columns are dominated by the June 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre and its regional echoes, alongside a domestic complaint about the government's refusal to grant autonomy to All India Radio and Doordarshan.

R. Srinivasan and S.V. Raju's lead essay on the Ninth General Elections argues voters chose on issues over personalities, attributing Rajiv Gandhi's early election call to fresh Bofors revelations and crediting the electorate with holding incumbents accountable regardless of caste or literacy.

Minoo Masani's "A Hung Parliament — The Beginning of Coalition Politics in India" welcomes the hung Parliament as normal rather than aberrant, criticises Devi Lal and Chandra Shekhar's manoeuvring against V.P. Singh's leadership bid, and argues rural voters grasped the Bofors/corruption issue better than the educated elite.

Contributors including R.S. Morkhandikar, Aloo J. Dastur, Mihir Sinha, Prema Nanda Kumar, Louella Lobo Prabhu, Babu Joseph, Geeta Doctor, Nitin Raut and Arvind Deshpande assess the November 1989 election results region by region, debating whether the hung Parliament marks the start of durable coalition politics in India.
The issue carries the Dalai Lama's Nobel Peace Prize acceptance statement, a Liberal International resolution on Tibet, and obituary tributes to Andrei Sakharov.
A 1966 C. Rajagopalachari piece on constitutional convention is reprinted from Swarajya, alongside the opening of M.N. Buch's essay on the Panchayat Raj Bill.

R. Srinivasan's "Degeneration of Higher Education" links urban teenage violence to collapsing family discipline and media glorification of violence, using two regional novels as sociological evidence of political patronage corrupting college admissions, and details a candidate's line-itemed election bribery budget.

P. L. Olatikar's "Turmoil in the Campus" argues the mass rush for college admission reflects parental anxiety rather than academic interest, and proposes vocationalisation of education after the 10th standard.

An unsigned piece by "A Teacher," "Urban Teenage Violence — The Danger Signals," catalogues flashpoints including the Rinku Patil murder and criticises both careerist teachers and moralising commentary that ignores adolescent frustration.

R. S. Morkhandikar's "The Decline of Education" traces how institutions founded by politician-educationists like Ambedkar and Panjabrao Deshmukh were captured from the 1960s onward by politicians seeking patronage over admissions to lucrative courses.

Will Durant's reprinted 1959 convocation address, "Advice to Youth," offers paternal counsel on health, marriage, and character, arguing modern civilisation has unwisely over-stimulated the sexual impulse.

The issue opens with a personal tribute to broadcaster Mehra Masani by P.C. Chatterji and frames its whole symposium around a spate of campus killings reflecting the degeneration of Indian higher education.

A Rajaji Foundation seminar report, "The Kashmir Problem — Time for a People's Initiative," argues decades of broken plebiscite promises and militant repression have alienated Kashmiris, and calls for a "people's initiative" letting Kashmiris themselves negotiate their future.

Minoo Masani's seminar remarks go further, calling "integral part of India" a hollow slogan and urging India to offer Kashmir a genuine choice, including independence, drawing an analogy to Gorbachev's stance on Baltic sovereignty.

H. M. Seervai's "The Crisis in the Judiciary" argues judicial corruption is especially corrosive because it removes society's last institutional defence, insisting a corrupt judge deserves no special leniency from ordinary criminal prosecution.

Louella Lobo Prabhu's "Corruption in the Higher Judiciary" catalogues specific scandals — a bag of currency in a judge's ante-chamber, a no-confidence motion by Bar members — and traces politicised appointments to Indira Gandhi's "committed judiciary" doctrine.

The issue also carries S.V. Raju's editorial "The Liberal Conspiracy," Rani Sircar's housewife's-perspective critique of Congress, Bhanu Pratap Singh's agricultural-policy guidelines, and Chinese dissident Fang Lizhi's "Keeping the Faith."

Minoo Masani's "Do We Deserve our Prime Ministers?" indicts Rajiv Gandhi, V.P. Singh and Chandra Shekhar as each unfit, proposing a caretaker government of eminent non-political citizens like Justice H.R. Khanna pending fresh elections.
R. Swaminathan's "Prime Minister — Anyone?" argues India's leaders "don't know why they want power," detailing the Congress(I)'s calculated decision to prop up Chandra Shekhar's minority government.

F.A. Mechery and Maneesha Tikekar's "The Legitimacy of 'Arithmetical Democracy'" argue Chandra Shekhar's government has a legal case on arithmetic but lacks the legitimacy of a popular mandate, tracing defections that exploited gaps in the anti-defection law.

Gayatri Narayanan's "The Mandal Report — Some Reservations" argues public debate wrongly reduced the seven-volume Mandal Report to a single reservations clause, ignoring its educational-concession, land-reform, and Backward Classes Development Corporation recommendations.

Louella Lobo Prabhu's "The Ayodhya Non-Issue — An Avoidable Confrontation" lays out both the Muslim legal case and the Hindu psychological case on the Ram Janmabhoomi-Babri Masjid dispute, suggesting L.K. Advani's Rath Yatra was a calculated response to V.P. Singh's caste-based mobilisation.

A reprinted extract of B.R. Ambedkar's 25 November 1949 Constituent Assembly speech, "Will Democracy Survive in India?", warns against bhakti (hero-worship) in politics and insists political democracy is unsustainable without underlying social and economic democracy.

An unsigned assessment of the Mandal Commission's fallout, including student self-immolations, presents both the pro- and anti-reservation cases and concludes the country has reached "a point of divide."

The cover feature reports on a March 1991 Freedom First Foundation seminar on "India and the Gulf War," criticising India's confused diplomatic response, including the refuelling controversy, and pro-Saddam sympathies among sections of the Indian intelligentsia.

The seminar's consensus recommendations include rejecting the "unipolar world" thesis, strengthening the UN and Security Council, reorienting non-alignment away from anti-Americanism, building SAARC on an ECM model, and dropping India's one-sided Palestine position in favour of ties with Israel.

M. A. Rane's "Strengthen the United Nations" distinguishes criticising pro-Saddam sympathisers from endorsing US conduct, and argues the war's near-unanimous Security Council backing reflected shared oil interests rather than principle.

Nitin G. Raut's "Rethinking India's Foreign Policy" argues Nehruvian non-alignment tilted toward Moscow made India a "voluntary satellite of the USSR," crediting Chandrashekhar's restraint over Rajiv Gandhi's "immature" freelance peace diplomacy.
V.S. Sheth's "NAM Has a Role to Play" argues the Non-Aligned Movement, though politically weakened, retains a role in brokering a fairer international arrangement for Gulf oil resources.

Minoo Masani pays tribute to J.R.D. Tata on his retirement as Chairman of Tata Sons, and the issue carries a "Twenty Questions to Ask Your Candidate" election checklist from the Freedom First Foundation.

J.B. D'Souza argues Indian institutions from the bureaucracy to the judiciary have decayed under four decades of Congress rule, illustrating this with a sub-collector punished for helping exploited forest workers and corruption allegations against Bombay High Court judges.

Bhanu Pratap Singh presents statistical tables showing static or declining real returns to wheat and rice growers between 1970-71 and 1988-89 despite productivity gains, arguing Nehruvian development strategy systematically drained wealth from agriculture.
S. Ambirajan questions whether "stability" is a coherent policy goal at all, noting India's year-to-year per capita income growth ranged from -8.7% to 20.5% despite averaging about 4%.

A reprinted Economist Survey extract, "India — The Tiger Caged," rejects population growth as an adequate excuse for India's underperformance against Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Indonesia, diagnosing a state that has "done far too much and far too little."
A companion Sunday Times piece, "Home Truths for India," blames Fabian-socialist policy inherited from the Nehru-Gandhi family for import bans, licensing, and entrenched bureaucratic corruption.

An unsigned analysis, "BJP — The New Bogey-man of Indian Politics," questions alarmist readings of the BJP's rise after the tenth general election, arguing its gains reflect local political factors as much as a "Hindu wave."

A reprinted Amnesty International 1991 report on India's human-rights record, headlined "What Doordarshan Didn't Want You to Know," documents torture and extrajudicial killings in Punjab, Kashmir, Assam and post-Ayodhya violence.

A report on a Freedom First Foundation seminar, "The Indian Economy - Grappling with Realities - At Last," frames the 1991 reforms as the defeat of statism by economic reality and welcomes them as vindication of positions the magazine held for 39 years.

The concluding instalment of The Economist's "Survey of India" catalogues the mechanics of the licence-permit raj, cites Robert Wade's research on a "market for public office" in irrigation departments, and links economic grievance to separatist violence in Punjab, Kashmir and Assam.

A signed review credited to "An Economist" of Bimal Jalan's "India's Economic Crisis: The Way Ahead" praises the book's diagnosis but criticises its prescriptions as timid and rooted in an assumption that the state should retain a dominant economic role.
The seminar report poses open questions about whether reform will solve mass poverty and whether India should emulate a Korea-style growth model or a Scandinavian welfare-blended one.
The issue carries an In Memoriam section for Liberal International's Giovanni Malagodi, R.V. Murthy, and press baron Ramnath Goenka.

Vasundhara Mohan's "The Coup in the USSR" traces Gorbachev's reform record from 1985, credits the repeal of Article 6 as "the last straw" provoking hardliners, and recounts the failed August 1991 coup and Yeltsin's rise.

A.G. Modak's "Why the Coup Failed?" identifies four causes of Soviet communism's collapse — dogmatism, statism, exposure to "the truth about the West," and the exhaustion of militant materialist philosophy.

Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn's "Can Democracy Grow in Russia?" cautions that durable Russian democracy must be built bottom-up from local self-government, citing Karl Popper's view that democracy is chosen to avoid tyranny rather than for its virtues.

Fang Lizhi's "The Unfinished Revolution — China's Time Will Come" insists modernisation is impossible without democratisation, citing at least 876 Chinese labour camps and calling Tiananmen only "the tip of the iceberg."
A boxed commentary by Leszek Kolakowski cautions that denationalisation need not mean total privatisation and that market forces alone cannot resolve every social conflict.

The issue is dedicated to Mikhail Gorbachev and carries a column on forced blood donation by Tibetan prisoners in Chinese custody and a short obituary-styled essay, "Soviet Communism (1917–1991)," by Robert Conquest.

J.B. D'Souza's "Bureaucracy in the New Order" argues civil-service negativity and delay remain the biggest threat to liberalisation, citing the JJ Hospital glycerine poisoning case and Justice B. Lentin's inquiry as evidence that culpable officials are shielded or promoted.

Jiban K. Mukhopadhyay defends the 1991-92 reforms as unavoidable given the debt and deficit dynamics that brought India to the IMF and World Bank, warning that reform-era inflation near 14% falls hardest on the poorest three-quarters of the population.

D. R. Pendse's review of the 1992-93 Union Budget frames it as a further step toward de facto rupee convertibility via LERMS, praising Finance Minister Manmohan Singh as "a dextrous economist" while listing five outstanding reform areas.

A seminar report on "Obstacles to Liberalisation," featuring Gurcharan Das and D.N. Patodia, records agreement that forty years of state socialism had failed and warns vested interests could scuttle honest implementation of reform.

M.S. Srinivasan's "Representing the People — How much Our MPs Cost Us" itemises Parliament's perquisites at roughly Rs. 30 crore a year and proposes a ten-point reform including a Rs. 3,000/month salary cap and a contributory provident fund in place of pensions.

Minoo Masani's regular column welcomes India's establishment of full diplomatic relations with Israel and opposes a proposed government-sponsored history of independent India as improperly politicised.

D.N. Patodia's "The Reforms so Far — What Remains to be Done" credits the Rao government with delicensing roughly 80% of industries and permitting up to 50% foreign equity, while arguing further work is needed on cutting wasteful expenditure and reforming education and employment policy.

D. R. Pendse, interviewed by Economic Reforms Today, calls for an independent, Washington-style think tank to build public support for reform and expresses confidence India could be a major Asian economic force by 2005-2010 given consistent policy.

Minoo Masani's regular column condemns Pakistan's torture of an Indian diplomat, recalls his own 1960s Road Transport Reorganisation Committee recommendation to abolish octroi on petrol, and calls India's population growth to 844 million a symptom of the government's "utter failure" to control it.

A.G. Nadkarni analyses the Harshad Mehta securities scam — the largest Indian financial fraud since the 1950s Mundhra scandal — attributing it to systemic bank-nationalisation failures and calling for denationalisation of banking.

M.S. Srinivasan proposes cutting politicians' role down to properly political matters, delegating economic, social and educational policy to specialist independent commissions such as a forty-member National Economic Commission barred to politicians.

S.V. Raju's editorial "'Stray Incidents' Did You Say, Mr. Home Minister?" rebuts Home Minister S.B. Chavan's dismissal of human-rights abuses, citing playwright Vijay Tendulkar's public-interest petition and specific police-brutality cases to argue Amnesty International's criticism has substance.

Jamshed N. Guzder's biographical tribute traces Dadabhai Naoroji's life from founding girls' schools in 1849 Bombay through his 1892 election as the first Indian MP in the British House of Commons to his mentorship of a young Gandhi in South Africa.

Adi Doctor's "Dadabhai — The Secular Nationalist" contrasts Naoroji's secular, rights-based nationalism against the religio-spiritual nationalism of Tilak and Aurobindo, and explains his "drain of wealth" theory of British extraction from India.

V.S. Srinivasa Sastri's reprinted "Dadabhai in the House of Commons" recounts Naoroji's narrow three-vote 1892 election victory and his parliamentary work on simultaneous ICS examinations and the Welby Commission on Indo-British finances.

Minoo Masani's column praises Captain Lakshmi of the INA for refusing a Quit India commemorative award, supports a separate Jharkhand state for Adivasis, and condemns Iran's persecution of the Baha'i community.

The cover feature on the environment opens with Chief Seattle's 1854 letter and reports on the World Bank's independent "Morse Committee" review finding the Sardar Sarovar Narmada project's resettlement programme inadequate, accompanied by Medha Patkar's "Narmada Action Alert."

The lead feature reports on a January 9, 1993 emergency seminar on secularism held amid curfew and Bombay's post-Babri Masjid riots, with 51 participants questioning whether pre-modern India was ever genuinely tolerant.

M.S. Gore directly disputes that sarva-dharma-samabhava (equal regard for all religions) is consistent with a secular ethic, arguing genuine secularism requires treating religion as irrelevant to individual opportunity.
Minoo Masani argues India should be "non-denominational, not secular," proposing only Republic Day and Independence Day as universal holidays.
Ruchira Gupta's eyewitness account describes the December 6, 1992 demolition of the Babri Masjid, kar sevaks assaulting journalists, and her own near-lynching when identified as Muslim.
The seminar's Uniform Civil Code discussion reproduces a 1986 Indian Secular Society draft proposal, with Justice V.D. Tulzapurkar, recommending abolition of polygamy and unilateral divorce.

Reprinted historical material includes a 1679 letter from Shivaji to Aurangzeb pleading for religious tolerance and Babar's 1529 "secret will" to Humayun urging the same, alongside B.T. Dastur's polemic on India's "relapse into savagery."
A contribution from a Muslim Satyashodak Mandal activist describes the "dilemma of progressive Muslims," accused of teaching Islam when raising reform and of anti-Islamic bias when criticising it.

R. Srinivasan's "The Criminalisation of Politics in India" argues the March 1993 Bombay bomb blasts confirmed a long-recognised trend, tracing it from election-cost financing through the Emergency-era Youth Congress to today's criminal-politician nexus.

S.V. Raju's "Criminal Politicians or Political Criminals?" documents corporators and MLAs across Bombay, Aurangabad and Nagpur facing criminal charges, including alleged links between Vasai-Virar politician Hitendra Thakur's family and Dawood Ibrahim, and favours the 1957 Second Five Year Plan's licence-permit-quota regime as the root cause.

V.C. Phadke's "Keeping the Peace the Bhiwandi Way" explains why Bhiwandi, despite past riots, stayed peaceful during the December 1992-January 1993 violence, crediting mohalla committees and joint Hindu-Muslim patrols as a replicable "Bhiwandi Model."

Mervyn Hiskett's "Democracy or Theocracy" argues a recurring Islamic predisposition against secular pluralism has produced conflict from Partition-era India to 1980s Nigeria and Sudan, citing the Indian Muslim League's rejection of Gandhian secular nationalism.

A.G. Philip's piece under "The Masani Viewpoint" argues Hindutva-style politics is a mobile prejudice that merely finds new targets, comparing the Shiv Sena's shift from south Indians to Muslims with Pakistan's turn against Bengalis after Partition.
The issue also tributes the Sarajevo newspaper Oslobodenje, nominated by the Indian Liberal Group for the Liberal International 1993 Prize for Freedom.

B. N. Mehrish reports on the UN World Conference on Human Rights in Vienna (June 1993), noting the UN Centre for Human Rights received over 125,000 complaints that year, nearly triple 1992's total, and detailing the Vienna Declaration's action programme.

S. V. Raju's obituary for Irene d'Avoine recounts her father Dr. Charles d'Avoine's career as a Bombay rationalist tried and acquitted in 1933 under IPC Section 295, with both father and daughter buried without religious rites.

V. C. Phadke reports on an essay exercise given to 300 Bhiwandi college students on the 1992-93 communal riots, finding many blamed religious fanaticism and opportunistic politicians while also invoking Gandhian universalism.

Adi Doctor reviews Osborne and Gaebler's "Reinventing Government," explaining "entrepreneurial government" that steers rather than rows, citing New Zealand's airline deregulation and Chicago's parent-controlled school councils.

The Dalai Lama's statement on the 34th anniversary of the Tibetan uprising warns that China's new "special economic zone" status for the Tibet Autonomous Region risks accelerating demographic and cultural assimilation.

Minoo Masani's column pays personal tribute to his late sister Mehra Masani, a senior All India Radio official denied the Director-General post, and criticises a Supreme Court decision permitting fee-based reservation of college seats after a student suicide over an unaffordable donation.

A satirical piece by S. S. Bankeshwar "interviews" a suitcase personifying cash-bribe politics after the Harshad Mehta scandal, referencing the Rs. 67 lakh suitcase allegedly delivered to PM Narasimha Rao.

G. Narayanaswamy's Rajaji Birthday Lecture recounts C. Rajagopalachari's Vedantic philosophy of detached duty and his record as Madras Chief Minister opening the Meenakshi Temple to Harijans and pioneering prohibition.

K. S. Ramamurthy's "Kashmir - The Way Out" argues India should honour its 1948 commitment to a free plebiscite, citing N. Gopalswamy Iyengar's UN Security Council pledge and Article 370 as evidence India never treated the accession as final.

A reprinted Swiss Press Review piece, "The Solution: An Independent Kashmir," argues neither the Indian nor Pakistani position serves Kashmiris and recalls Nehru's near-agreement with Ayub Khan on independence with joint neutrality guarantees before his death.

Ashok V. Chowgule's rebuttal defends the Indian Army's conduct in Kashmir against Bernard Levin's earlier accusations, citing the Verghese Committee's finding that reports of Army excesses were "grossly exaggerated or invented."

Minoo Masani's "An Open Letter to My Younger Friends" recalls founding the Swatantra Party with Rajaji in 1959 and appeals to a younger generation to organise a movement keeping economic liberalisation from stalling.

Resolutions of the Fifth Shetkari Sanghatana Convention at Aurangabad blame the Latur-Osmanabad earthquake's toll on anti-farmer housing policy and demand abolition of agricultural pricing controls and restoration of constitutional property rights.

An obituary tribute to H. M. Patel recounts his roles reorganising the armed forces after Partition, founding LIC, and serving as Swatantra Party president and Janata-government Finance and Home Minister.

Yogesh Kamdar's tribute to Justice N.P. Nathwani recounts his defence, then public renunciation, of the Preventive Detention Act, his Emergency-era free-speech victory, and his 1978 inquiry into repression of the Dawoodi Bohra community.

S.V. Raju's explainer defends India's April 1994 signing of the GATT Marrakesh accord against protectionist and sovereignty-based objections, tracing GATT's history since 1947 and its impending conversion into the World Trade Organisation.

Sharad Joshi's essay on "ulti-patti" (reverse settlement), opening with his own experience of being billed rather than paid for cucumbers, estimates Indian farmers' annual loss from unremunerative pricing at Rs. 12,000 crores and links this history of implicit farm taxation to the GATT agricultural negotiations.

Sharad Bailur's "The Great American Bubble" criticises U.S. passage of NAFTA and warns that America's "credit card economy" of proliferating consumer debt underlies a broader fragility in the world economy.

Minoo Masani's column criticises federal overreach in choosing Gujarat's Chief Minister, praises T. N. Seshan's independence as Chief Election Commissioner, and announces the planned launch of the Swatantra Bharat movement in Nagpur.

Tributes mark the deaths of industrialist S. L. Kirloskar, who favoured abolishing the Planning Commission and FERA, and scholar Tarkateerth Laxmanshastri Joshi, who campaigned against untouchability.

S. V. Raju's "The Return of Swatantra" reports on Sharad Joshi's founding of the new political party Swatantra Bharat, prompted by Minoo Masani's appeal, with a thirty-point transitional programme covering law and order, pruning the state, and privatisation.

V. K. Sinha's profile of Taslima Nasreen presents her as a Bangladeshi physician and writer facing a fundamentalist fatwa and bounty over her novel Lajja, arguing, via Philip Green, that free speech is constitutive of democracy while religious sentiment is merely incidental to it.
Gwynne Dyer's "Islamic Feminism" contrasts female heads of government in Pakistan, Bangladesh and Turkey with ongoing fundamentalist violence in Algeria, Egypt and Sudan.

An unsigned report on the Shetkari Mahila Aghadi's Lakshmi-Mukti movement describes the transfer of agricultural land titles to rural housewives in Maharashtra, with over a thousand villages qualifying by February 1992.

Dilip Thakore's "A Testimony of Shame" reviews the UNDP's 1994 Human Development Report ranking India 135th of 173 nations, blaming the "mother of all errors" — the centrally planned socialist model — for entrenching an "amoral" middle class in political power.

Rajesh M. Basrur's essay on Indian national identity, cut off mid-argument, argues the real sources of national unease over Assam, Punjab, Kashmir and Ayodhya lie within Indian society rather than external threats.
"Of Cabbages & Kings" recounts the parable of "Sami," a self-censoring journalist, and the case of Egyptian professor Dr. Nasr Abu-Zaid, blocked from promotion and accused of apostasy.
